title: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
summary: How Chameleon, Emu3, Transfusion, Show-o, Janus and BAGEL put text and images in one sequence: discrete vs continuous images, autoregressive vs diffusion heads, encoders, masks and evaluation.
outcomes: Compute how many sequence positions an image takes for a given resolution and tokenizer downsampling
Explain why early-fusion training diverges and how QK-Norm, z-loss and norm reordering fix it
Build a causal and a Transfusion-style attention mask for a mixed sequence and explain when each is legal
Combine a next-token loss and a diffusion loss with a weight lambda and interpret the result
Compare shared vs decoupled encoders and read GenEval and understanding results fairly

lessons.title: Why one transformer should both read and draw images

blocks.md: Most multimodal systems are two specialists glued together. A **vision-language model** (VLM) such as LLaVA puts a vision encoder in front of an LLM: it can *read* an image and answer in text, but it cannot output pixels. A text-to-image **diffusion model** can *draw*, but it cannot hold a conversation or explain what it drew.

The obvious fix is a pipeline: the LLM writes a prompt string and calls a separate image generator as a tool. That works, but everything the generator knows about the conversation has to squeeze through a short text prompt. It cannot see the earlier images in the chat, and the LLM never sees the generator's internal state. A **unified multimodal model** removes the seam: one transformer reads and writes text and images in a single interleaved sequence, so an image can be generated in the middle of a paragraph and then discussed in the next sentence.

blocks.title: From glued specialists to one sequence model

nodes.label:
One transformer over
text + image tokens

scenes.caption: A vision-language model: image features flow into the LLM, and only text comes out. It can describe a picture but never produce one.
Add a separate generator as a tool. The only link is a short prompt string, so the generator sees none of the earlier images or conversation detail.
Unified model: a single transformer consumes and emits both modalities in one sequence and one context. Every design in this course is a different way to build this box.

blocks.md: Three prerequisites carry the whole course. From **building a GPT**: a decoder-only transformer with a causal mask, trained by next-token cross-entropy. From **visual tokenizers**: an encoder that shrinks an image by a downsampling factor $f$ into a grid of latents, either discrete codebook ids (VQ) or continuous vectors (a VAE). From **flow matching**: a network trained with a mean squared error to turn noise into data over several steps.

The first design question is cost. A tokenizer with downsampling $f$ turns an $H \times W$ image into $(H/f)(W/f)$ positions. With $f = 16$, a $256 \times 256$ image becomes a $16 \times 16$ grid: **256 tokens**, plus a begin-of-image (BOI) and end-of-image (EOI) marker, so 258 positions. Chameleon's tokenizer maps $512 \times 512$ to 1024 tokens (also $f = 16$); Emu3's maps $512 \times 512$ to 4096 tokens ($f = 8$).

blocks.caption: Image positions in the sequence for a tokenizer with spatial downsampling f (markers not counted).

scenes.caption: At f = 16 the curve passes through the toy (256 px, 256 tokens), Janus's 384 px generation grid (576 tokens) and Chameleon (512 px, 1024 tokens).
At f = 8 every image costs 4x more tokens: Emu3's 512 px image is 4096 tokens. Doubling the side length always quadruples the count.
At f = 32 a 512 px image is only 256 tokens, but each token must now summarize a 32 x 32 pixel patch, so reconstructions lose detail.

blocks.md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

blocks.question: A tokenizer downsamples by 16 in each direction. How many image positions does a 512 x 512 image take, not counting BOI and EOI?
blocks.explain: 512 / 16 = 32 per side, and 32 x 32 = 1024. This matches Chameleon, whose tokenizer turns a 512 x 512 image into 1024 tokens. 32 is only one side; 4096 is what an f = 8 tokenizer gives.

blocks.question: Why does a unified model beat an LLM that calls a separate image generator through a text prompt, for a request like "make the dog in the previous picture wear a hat"?
options: The unified model has more parameters in total
Diffusion models cannot generate dogs
The generator only sees the prompt string, not the earlier image, while a unified model attends to the earlier image tokens directly
Tool calls are not allowed during generation
blocks.explain: The bottleneck is information, not size. In a pipeline the generator conditions only on what fits in the prompt. In a unified model the earlier image is part of the same context, so the new image can attend to it.

lessons.title: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3

blocks.md: The simplest unified model treats an image exactly like text. A VQ tokenizer turns the image into a grid of codebook ids, the ids are read in raster order (left to right, top to bottom), and they are dropped into the same sequence as the text tokens. One vocabulary, one embedding table, one transformer, one loss: next-token cross-entropy over every position. Chameleon (Meta FAIR, 2024) calls this **early fusion**, because the modalities are mixed from the first layer instead of being encoded separately and fused late.

Chameleon's image tokenizer encodes a $512 \times 512$ image into 1024 tokens from a codebook of 8192 entries. Its BPE text vocabulary has 65,536 entries, and that number *includes* the 8192 image codes. So generating an image is literally sampling 1024 more tokens, just from a different slice of the vocabulary. Emu3 (BAAI, 2024) pushes the same idea to video: its tokenizer turns a $512 \times 512$ image (or a 4-frame clip) into 4096 tokens from a 32,768-entry codebook, and the paper's title states the thesis: next-token prediction is all you need.

blocks.title: A mixed sequence in one shared vocabulary

scenes.caption: Toy sequence: 5 text tokens and a 2 x 2 image (4 codebook ids) wrapped in BOI and EOI markers. Simplified: a real 256 px image at f = 16 has 256 image tokens, not 4.
Early fusion: every position, text or image, goes through the same embedding table and transformer. Image ids are just a reserved range of the vocabulary.
Training is plain next-token prediction. The output at position 4 (p1) is scored on predicting p2, exactly as the output at 'a' is scored on predicting 'red'.
Generation: once the model samples BOI, it samples image ids one at a time (4 here, 1024 for Chameleon at 512 px), then EOI, then text again. The VQ decoder turns ids back into pixels.

blocks.md: The price of discreteness is information. Each Chameleon image token is one of 8192 codes, which is $\log_2 8192 = 13$ bits. 1024 tokens x 13 bits = 13,312 bits, about 1.7 KB, to describe an image whose raw RGB bytes take 786,432 bytes, a ratio of about 473 to 1. The Chameleon paper itself names the weakness: its tokenizer struggles to reconstruct images with a lot of text, which caps the model on OCR-heavy tasks.

blocks.caption: Upper bound on the information in one Chameleon image, compared with the raw pixels.

blocks.md: Training was not easy. Chameleon reports that with all weights shared, each modality tries to "compete" by slowly growing its norms. Softmax ignores a constant shift, $\mathrm{softmax}(z) = \mathrm{softmax}(z + c)$, so nothing in the loss stops logits from drifting upward until they leave bf16's useful range and training diverges. Ablations *without* image generation did not diverge.

blocks.title: Softmax cannot see a logit shift, z-loss can

scenes.caption: Logits (2, 1, 0) give probabilities 0.665, 0.245, 0.090. Here log Z = 2.408 and the z-loss term 1e-5 (log Z)^2 is about 0.00006.
Shift every logit by 100: (102, 101, 100). The probabilities are identical, so cross-entropy is identical. But log Z = 102.408 and the z-loss is about 0.105, so the drift is now penalized.

blocks.md:
Chameleon's fixes, all from its stability section:

- **QK-Norm**: a layer norm on queries and keys inside attention, which bounds the input to the attention softmax. Without it, Chameleon-7B diverged after about 20% of an epoch.
- **z-loss**: add $10^{-5} \log^2 Z$ to the loss, where $Z$ is the output softmax's normalizer. This targets the final softmax, which QK-Norm does not touch.
- **Dropout** 0.1 for the 7B model, and for the 34B model a **reordered norm** (the Swin Transformer placement, normalizing each block's output before the residual add) to bound the feed-forward block's growth.
Chameleon found that uncontrolled growth of the last layer's output norm predicted a divergence that could appear 20 to 30% into training. Monitor output norms, not just the loss curve.

Misconception: "sharing a vocabulary makes images and text equally easy to model." Image tokens have very different entropy from text tokens, and the paper attributes the instability exactly to modalities of different entropy sharing one softmax.

blocks.question: Chameleon-7B diverged without QK-Norm, and an ablation without image generation did not diverge. Which explanation does the paper give?
options: Sharing all weights across modalities of different entropy lets norms grow, and softmax's shift invariance means the loss does not resist it
Image tokens have a larger vocabulary than text tokens
The VQ decoder sends exploding gradients back into the transformer
Images are longer than text, so the learning rate is too high
blocks.explain: Softmax(z) = softmax(z + c), so a uniform growth in logits costs nothing in cross-entropy, and with modalities competing the norms creep up until bf16 overflows. QK-Norm and z-loss add the missing resistance. The tokenizer is frozen, so it sends no gradients.

blocks.question: A product team wants a Chameleon-style model to read dense receipts and screenshots. What is the main risk the Chameleon paper itself points to?
options: Next-token prediction cannot model 2D layouts at all
The model cannot attend from text to image tokens
The vocabulary has no room for more image codes
The discrete tokenizer reconstructs text-heavy images poorly, which upper-bounds OCR quality
blocks.explain: With 13 bits per token and 1024 tokens per 512 px image, fine glyph detail is the first thing lost. The paper calls this a core weakness that bounds OCR-heavy tasks. Separate understanding encoders (lesson 5) are one answer.

lessons.title: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences

blocks.md: A GPT uses a **causal mask**: position $i$ may attend to positions $j \le i$. That is required for text, because at generation time token $i+1$ does not exist yet. But an image has no natural left-to-right order. Raster order is a convention, and under a causal mask the top-left patch never sees the bottom-right one.

Transfusion (Meta, Zhou et al., 2024) keeps causal attention for every element but adds **bidirectional attention within each image**: every patch of an image may attend to every other patch of the same image, while still only seeing text and images that came *before* it. This is safe because, as the next lesson shows, Transfusion generates all patches of an image together, so no patch depends on a patch that does not exist yet.

blocks.prompt: Take the toy sequence: a, red, cube, BOI, p1, p2, p3, p4, EOI, on, sand (11 positions). A causal mask allows 66 query-key pairs. How many pairs does the Transfusion mask allow?
blocks.reveal: **72.** The causal mask allows $1 + 2 + \dots + 11 = 66$ pairs. Bidirectional attention inside the image adds the pairs where an earlier patch looks at a later one: (p1,p2), (p1,p3), (p1,p4), (p2,p3), (p2,p4), (p3,p4), which is $\binom{4}{2} = 6$. Nothing else changes: text before the image still cannot see it, and text after it sees everything.

blocks.title: Causal mask vs Transfusion mask (rows attend to columns)

scenes.caption: Causal mask: 66 allowed pairs (1 = may attend). Row p1 sees only a, red, cube, BOI and itself: 5 keys. The first patch is drawn without knowing anything about the other three.
Under the causal mask the patches see 5, 6, 7 and 8 keys. Information only flows from earlier patches to later ones, an arbitrary raster order imposed on a 2D grid.
Transfusion mask: the 4 x 4 image block is fully open. The 6 highlighted cells are new, giving 72 allowed pairs. Every patch now sees all 8 keys: the text, BOI and all four patches.
Rows before the image are unchanged: 'cube' still cannot see any patch. Rows after the image ('on', 'sand') see all of it, so text can describe the image it follows.
Show-o's omni-attention gives this same pattern for text-to-image: causal text, full attention among image tokens. Chameleon, Emu3 and Janus keep the plain causal mask throughout.

blocks.md: Does it matter? Transfusion's ablation on a 0.76B model with linear patch layers says yes: switching from causal to intra-image bidirectional attention dropped COCO FID (lower is better) from **61.3 to 20.3** and raised the captioning score CIDEr (higher is better) from 12.7 to 16.0, with text perplexity unchanged. With U-Net patch layers the gap mostly vanished (16.8 vs 16.7 FID), because the U-Net blocks already mix information across the whole image regardless of the transformer's mask.

Masks get richer when a model keeps several copies of an image. BAGEL (ByteDance Seed, 2025) feeds each training image as noised VAE tokens (for the generation loss), clean VAE tokens and ViT tokens (for conditioning). Its **generalized causal attention** lets later tokens attend to the clean and ViT copies of earlier images but never to the noised copy, and inside each split text stays causal while vision tokens are bidirectional.

The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

blocks.question: A colleague changes the mask so the text token 'cube' (before BOI) can attend to p1 to p4 during training. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, more attention is always better
Information leaks: training uses image content that will not exist when 'cube' is generated, so train and inference disagree
The model runs out of memory
The image patches can no longer see the text
blocks.explain: At inference the caption comes before the image, so when 'cube' is produced there are no patches yet. A mask that lets 'cube' read them teaches the model to rely on information it will never have. The fix is to keep the rows before BOI strictly causal.

blocks.question: Why can Transfusion open up attention inside the image when Chameleon cannot?
options: Transfusion uses a larger context window
Chameleon images are smaller
Transfusion denoises all patches of an image at once, so every patch exists at every step, whereas Chameleon emits patches one by one
Transfusion has no text tokens inside images
blocks.explain: In a diffusion step all n patches (noisy versions of them) are in the sequence simultaneously, so a patch attending to a later patch reads something real. In token-by-token generation a later patch has not been sampled yet, so letting an earlier one see it during training would be a leak.

lessons.title: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses

blocks.md: Lesson 2 paid for discreteness with 13 bits per token. Transfusion keeps images **continuous**. An 86M-parameter VAE turns a $256 \times 256$ image into a $32 \times 32 \times 8$ latent (each 8-dim latent pixel stands for an $8 \times 8$ pixel patch). The latent is cut into $2 \times 2$ patches, giving $16 \times 16 = 256$ patch vectors, each projected into the transformer by a linear layer or U-Net down blocks. Patch sizes of 1, 2, 4 or 8 latent pixels give 1024, 256, 64 or 16 positions per image: larger patches mean fewer positions.

Training adds noise to the whole latent, then the same transformer predicts that noise at the image's patch positions. Text positions get the usual next-token cross-entropy; image patches get a DDPM loss (mean squared error between true and predicted noise), computed once per image. The two are simply added:

blocks.caption: Transfusion's objective. The paper sets lambda to 5 after preliminary experiments and leaves tuning to future work. No loss is computed at the BOI position.

blocks.md: **Worked example.** Take the toy sequence. Say the model gives the correct next text token probabilities 0.40, 0.25, 0.60, 0.50 and 0.30 at the five text predictions. Cross-entropies are $-\ln p$: 0.916, 1.386, 0.511, 0.693, 1.204, so $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} = 0.942$. The 2 x 2 image has four 2-dim noise vectors; true $\epsilon$ = (0.5, -1.0), (1.2, 0.3), (-0.4, 0.8), (0.0, -0.6) and predicted = (0.3, -0.7), (0.9, 0.5), (-0.1, 0.6), (0.2, -0.2). Squared errors per patch are 0.13, 0.13, 0.13, 0.20, and the mean over all 8 numbers is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DDPM}} = 0.074$.

blocks.title: Combining the losses for the toy sequence

scenes.caption: The raw terms: text cross-entropy 0.942 and image noise MSE 0.074. They are on very different scales, so a plain sum would let text dominate the gradient.
With lambda = 1: total = 0.942 + 0.074 = 1.016. The image term is about 7% of the objective.
With Transfusion's lambda = 5: 5 x 0.07375 = 0.369, total = 1.311. The image now contributes about 28% of the loss. Simplified toy numbers, chosen to show the arithmetic.

blocks.md: At inference Transfusion switches modes. In **LM mode** it samples text token by token. When it samples BOI it enters **diffusion mode**: it appends $n$ patches of pure noise and denoises them for $T$ steps, each step overwriting the patches in place, so the model only ever sees the latest noise level. Then it appends EOI and returns to LM mode. The paper samples with 250 diffusion steps (training used 1000 timesteps).

blocks.title: Transfusion decoding switches between two modes

scenes.caption: LM mode: three forward passes sample 'a', 'red', 'cube', then the model samples BOI.
Diffusion mode: append all 4 noisy patches and denoise them together. Each pass updates every patch at once. Simplified: 4 steps here, 250 in the paper.
Diffusion done: append EOI and go back to LM mode for 'on' and 'sand', which attend to the clean finished image.

blocks.md: Results from the paper: in a controlled comparison with the Chameleon recipe, Transfusion exceeded Chameleon's text-to-image quality at less than a third of the compute and matched its image captioning at 21.8% of the FLOPs. The 7B model trained on 2T tokens (1T text, about 1T image patches) reached GenEval 0.63. One subtlety: when an image comes *before* its caption, the caption is learning from a noised image. Capping the noise at $t = 500$ (half the schedule) for those 20% of pairs clearly improved captioning.

Two relatives. **Show-o** (Show Lab NUS and ByteDance, 2024) stays discrete but drops raster order: image tokens (256 per $256 \times 256$ image from an 8192-code MAGVIT-v2 style quantizer) are randomly replaced by a [MASK] token, and the model predicts the masked ones from text and the visible ones, MaskGIT style. Its loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{MTP}} + \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{NTP}}$. **BAGEL** uses rectified flow, the flow-matching objective from the prerequisite, on FLUX VAE latents (8x downsampling then 2 x 2 patches), and weights its losses CE : MSE = 0.25 : 1.

blocks.title: Show-o fills masked image tokens in parallel

scenes.caption: Generation starts with every image token set to [MASK] (M). Toy: 4 tokens; a real 256 px image has 256.
One pass predicts all masked positions at once; the most confident predictions are kept (toy codebook ids), the rest are masked again.
The next pass conditions on the kept tokens and fills the remaining ones. Image tokens attend to each other fully, as in the Transfusion mask.

blocks.md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

blocks.question: A Transfusion-style step has L_LM = 0.942 and L_DDPM = 0.07375. What is the total loss with lambda = 5?
blocks.explain: 0.942 + 5 x 0.07375 = 0.942 + 0.369 = 1.311. 1.016 is lambda = 1. 4.78 wrongly multiplies the text term by 5 instead (5 x 0.942 + 0.074 is about 4.78).

blocks.question: Why does capping the diffusion noise at t = 500 for image-before-caption pairs help captioning?
options: The caption tokens attend to the image, and with full noise they would often be describing near-pure noise
It halves the number of image tokens
It makes the image loss computed per token instead of per image
It switches the image to discrete tokens
blocks.explain: In training the image is noised for its own diffusion loss, and later tokens condition on that noisy version. When the caption follows the image, a heavily noised image hides the content to describe. Limiting noise keeps the image readable; the paper measured better CIDEr with under 1% effect elsewhere.

lessons.title: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing

blocks.md: Understanding and generation want different things from an image encoder. To answer "what is on the sign?", the model needs **semantic** features, like those from a contrastively trained ViT such as SigLIP. To draw, it needs a code that a decoder can turn back into exact pixels, which favors a **reconstruction** tokenizer like VQ. Forcing one encoder to serve both, as Chameleon and Show-o do by default, is a compromise.

Janus (DeepSeek-AI, 2024) **decouples visual encoding** while keeping one transformer. For understanding, a SigLIP-Large encoder at 384 px produces features that a 2-layer MLP adaptor maps into the LLM. For generation, a VQ tokenizer (codebook 16,384, downsampling 16) produces ids that another MLP adaptor embeds, and a separate, randomly initialized **image head** predicts the next image id. The LLM is DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B, and the whole model stays autoregressive with an ordinary causal mask.

blocks.title: Janus: two visual paths, one transformer

scenes.caption: Understanding: the image goes through SigLIP, the text through the LLM tokenizer, and the shared transformer answers through the ordinary text head.
Generation: the prompt enters as text; image ids are fed back through the VQ path and the image head predicts the next id. The VQ decoder renders the finished grid.

BAGEL keeps the same split (SigLIP2 ViT for understanding, a FLUX VAE for generation) but swaps the VQ path for continuous latents with a rectified-flow loss, and gives each task its own transformer expert with shared self-attention.

blocks.md: The Janus ablation (Table 5) isolates the effect. All rows train on understanding and generation together unless noted. MMBench (MMB) is a multiple-choice understanding benchmark, higher is better; COCO FID measures generation, lower is better.

blocks.title: Janus ablation: shared vs decoupled encoders

scenes.caption: MMBench. A shared VQ tokenizer scores 35.0. A shared semantic tokenizer reaches 52.7. Decoupled SigLIP + VQ reaches 69.4, close to the understanding-only SigLIP model (E, 70.6).
COCO FID (lower is better). Generation barely changes: 8.72, 7.11 and 8.53, and generation-only training (F) gives 8.92. The split mostly rescues understanding without hurting generation.

blocks.md: Janus generates with **classifier-free guidance** (CFG). During training the caption is replaced by a pad token 10% of the time, so the model also learns unconditional image logits $l_u$. At sampling time each image token uses $l_g = l_u + s(l_c - l_u)$ with $s = 5$ by default.

blocks.title: CFG sharpens the next image token

scenes.caption: Conditional logits l_c = (2.0, 1.0, 0.5) give probabilities 0.629, 0.231, 0.140.
Unconditional logits l_u = (1.5, 1.2, 0.4) give 0.482, 0.357, 0.161. Id B is more likely without the prompt than with it.
Guided with s = 5: l_g = (4.0, 0.2, 0.9), so probabilities 0.937, 0.021, 0.042. Tokens the prompt favors are boosted; tokens it argues against (B) are pushed down hard.

blocks.md: Janus-Pro (2025) keeps the architecture and scales data, training schedule and size to 1B and 7B. Janus-Pro-7B reports 79.2 on MMBench (Janus: 69.4) and 0.80 on GenEval (Janus: 0.61).

Shared vs separate encoders is a trade between simplicity and specialization. One encoder means one token type and one path, but semantic and reconstruction goals pull against each other. Two encoders let each path pick its best tool while the transformer still sees one sequence.

blocks.question: In the Janus ablation, replacing the shared VQ tokenizer with decoupled SigLIP + VQ raised MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4 while FID moved from 8.72 to 8.53. What does that suggest?
options: Generation quality was the bottleneck
The transformer was too small
A reconstruction-oriented tokenizer gives poor semantic features for understanding, and a dedicated understanding encoder fixes that without hurting generation
MMBench rewards image resolution only
blocks.explain: Generation was about the same in both rows, so the gain is almost all understanding. VQ codes are trained to rebuild pixels, not to expose meaning; SigLIP is trained to align images with text.

blocks.question: With Janus's CFG formula l_g = l_u + s(l_c - l_u), what does s = 1 give?
options: Pure unconditional sampling
Twice the guidance
Uniform probabilities
Exactly the conditional logits, no extra guidance
blocks.explain: With s = 1, l_g = l_u + l_c - l_u = l_c. s = 0 would be unconditional. Values above 1, like the default 5, push past the conditional distribution toward what the prompt specifically adds.

lessons.title: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design

blocks.md: A unified model has to be scored twice. For **understanding**, papers report VLM benchmarks: MMBench (multiple-choice perception and reasoning), POPE (object hallucination), MMMU (college-level multimodal questions), SEED-Bench and others. For **generation**, FID on COCO measures distribution match but rewards matching COCO's photo style, which is why the Show-o authors caution that it may not reflect fidelity well. Prompt-following needs its own test.

**GenEval** (Ghosh et al., 2023) checks whether the image contains what the prompt asked for. It has six tasks: single object, two objects, counting (2, 3 or 4), colors, position (above, below, left, right) and color attribution (binding two colors to two objects). A Mask2Former detector trained on COCO finds objects (confidence above 0.3, raised to 0.9 for counting), and a CLIP model classifies colors. The overall score is the mean over tasks, from 0 to 1.

blocks.title: GenEval overall, as reported in the papers

scenes.caption: Overall GenEval without prompt rewriting: Chameleon 0.39 (quoted by later papers), Emu3 0.54, Janus 0.61, Transfusion 0.63, Show-o 0.68, Janus-Pro-7B 0.80, BAGEL 0.82.

With an LLM rewriter (red bars), Emu3 reports 0.66 and BAGEL 0.88. Same benchmark, different protocol: compare only like with like. Earlier tones: b discrete shared, c discrete decoupled, a continuous.

blocks.title: Where models fail: GenEval per task

scenes.caption: Show-o (1.3B): near perfect on single objects (0.98) but weak on position (0.31) and color attribution (0.50).
Janus-Pro-7B: position jumps to 0.79 and color attribution to 0.66, yet counting (0.59) is below Show-o's 0.66. One overall number hides these trades.

blocks.md: GenEval prompts are short and templated, and some models are trained mostly on long synthetic captions. Emu3's authors say exactly this and report rewriter numbers too. Before comparing two papers, check the rewriter, the CFG scale, and whether numbers were measured or copied from another paper.

The design axes, side by side:

- **Image representation**: discrete tokens (Chameleon, Emu3, Show-o, Janus generation) give one loss and plain LLM infrastructure, but lose detail. Continuous latents (Transfusion, BAGEL) keep detail but need a second loss and a noise schedule.
- **Generation head**: token-by-token autoregression (Chameleon, Emu3, Janus) needs one pass per image token; masked prediction (Show-o) or diffusion and flow (Transfusion, BAGEL) generate all of an image's positions together over a fixed number of steps.
- **Encoders**: shared (Chameleon, Show-o default) vs separate for understanding and generation (Janus, BAGEL).
- **Attention mask**: plain causal vs causal with bidirectional blocks inside images (Transfusion, Show-o, BAGEL).

No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

blocks.question: Paper X reports GenEval 0.88 and paper Y reports 0.80. X used an LLM to rewrite prompts and Y did not. What is the right conclusion?
options: The scores are not directly comparable; compare X without the rewriter (if reported) to Y
X is clearly better at following prompts
Y must have used a weaker detector
GenEval scores above 0.8 are always saturated, so they tie
blocks.explain: Rewriting expands short prompts into detailed descriptions, which helps models trained on long captions. BAGEL reports 0.82 without and 0.88 with a rewriter; against Janus-Pro-7B's 0.80 the fair comparison is 0.82.

blocks.question: A team needs one model that reads screenshots with small text and also generates images that must preserve fine detail, and can afford extra architecture. Which combination best fits the evidence in this course?
options: One shared VQ tokenizer with a causal mask, for simplicity
Discrete tokens at f = 32 to save context
A separate semantic encoder for understanding plus continuous latents with a diffusion or flow loss for generation
Text-only LLM with an external OCR tool and no image generation
blocks.explain: Chameleon's paper flags OCR as a weakness of discrete tokens, Janus shows a dedicated understanding encoder lifts MMBench from 35.0 to 69.4, and Transfusion shows continuous latents beat discrete tokens on generation at equal compute. BAGEL combines these choices.
